html:
Rhodes is the largest of the Dodecanese islands of Greece, in the south-east Aegean near the coast of Turkey. Its main city, also called Rhodes, at the island's northern tip, was one of the great sea powers of the Hellenistic world.

Three older towns on the island joined to found the city in 408 BCE. Placed on the sea lanes between the Aegean, Egypt and the Levant, it grew rich on shipping, banking and the grain trade, and its wine went far in stamped jars; see olive oil and wine trade. Its sea law was copied for centuries.

  • In 305 and 304 BCE it held out against Demetrius in a famous siege, and from the sale of his abandoned siege engines it built the Colossus of Rhodes.
  • Its navy kept the sea clear of pirates. The Winged Victory of Samothrace stands on a ship's prow of Rhodian marble.
  • It was Rome's ally, but after the battle of Pydna in 168 BCE Rome punished it by making Delos a free port, which took away much of its trade.
  • Under Rome it was a place of learning; the future emperor Tiberius spent years there.

From 1310 the Knights Hospitaller ruled the island and built the walled old town that still stands. Suleiman the Magnificent took it after a long siege in 1522. Italy seized it in 1912, and it joined Greece in 1947.
sum: Rhodes is the largest of the Dodecanese islands of Greece, in the south-east Aegean near the coast of Turkey. Its main city, also called Rhodes, at the island's northern tip, was one of the great sea powers of the Hellenistic world.
